newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Pilgrims from around world pack Fatima shrine.
newsitem.headline: Pilgrims from around world pack Fatima shrine.

text.p: More than 250,000 pilgrims packed the Catholic shrine of Fatima on Tuesday to mark the 80th anniversary of the "apparition" of the Virgin Mary to three peasant children.

In spring sunshine, the huge square in front of the sanctuary was transformed into a sea of white handkerchiefs as the faithful gave the traditional greeting to the statue of the Virgin as it paraded before them.

Roman Catholics believe the Virgin Mary appeared to the three shepherd children at midday on May 13, 1917, the first of five monthly apparitions during which she delivered three prophecies. One of the three predictions has never been revealed.

Fatima is one of the most revered Roman Catholic sites and the annual celebrations between May and October draw thousands of pilgrims from as far afield as the United States, Japan and eastern Europe, particularly Poland.

Pope John Paul is Polish and is known for his devotion to the Virgin who he believes intervened to save him from an assassination attempt on May 13 1981 when he was shot and seriously wounded by Turkish gunman Ali Agca.
He has visited the shrine at Fatima twice, once in 1982 and again in 1991 when he came to give thanks for the fall of communism in eastern Europe.
According to the writings of sister Lucia, the sole surviving visionary, two of the Virgin's prophecies concerned the end of the First World War and the collapse of communism.
But the so-called "Third Secret of Fatima" has never been revealed by the Catholic hierachy, stirring speculation that it alluded to some future catastrophe.
However, a senior Vatican official said on a visit to Portugal last year that it contained nothing alarming.

While most pilgrims arrive in Fatima, 80 miles (130km) north of Lisbon, by bus or car, some Portuguese make the trip on foot as a sign of particular devotion or to fulfil a promise. Some even complete the final stretch on their knees along a special pathway.

"I had a difficult birth and I promised the Virgin Mary that I would come to Fatima if my son lived," said 17-year-old Catia Solange as she edged her way towards the shrine on her knees carrying her four-month-old baby.

Amelia de Conceicao, 78, said she had been coming to the shrine since she was 15 and that her father had been present at the last of the apparitions on October 15, 1917, when the sun was supposed to have "danced" in the sky in the so-called "miracle of the sun".
Among those present was Nobel Peace laureate Carlos Ximenes Belo, a bishop in East Timor, the troubled former Portuguese Pacific colony which has been occupied by Indonesia since 1976.
Belo told journalists that Fatima was "an appeal to peace, pardon and reconciliation."
But sister Lucia was not present. The nun, who recently celebrated her 90th birthday, hardly ever leaves the Carmelite convent in central Portugal which she entered in 1929.
